clue.text: One who is sure to fail as flat-sitter?

definitions.text: One who is sure to fail

blocks.clueFragment: One who is sure to fail
blocks.note: surface reading: a hopeless case, someone or something bound to come to nothing
setter's reading: a bird shot by a sportsman no longer flies but lies flat on the ground

explanation.surface: A doomed candidate is mocked as someone who just sits flat.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the joke: a shot bird lies flat, and the phrase for a dead bird is also the idiom for a lost cause.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes a plan or person with no chance whatever of success, a lost cause.

clue.text: Play-off to conclude with a single?

blocks.note: to conclude is to settle or make up one's mind
in cricket a single is one run, and R is the scorecard abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A play-off match is won by scoring one more run at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: A single is a cricket term: one run, scored by running once between the wickets.
explanation.definitionFit: An extra game held to break a tie between level teams is called by this term.

clue.text: “Blithe Spirit” is impractical

blocks.note: blithe and carefree, light-hearted
a fairy is a magical spirit

explanation.surface: A critic calls Noel Coward's comedy Blithe Spirit an unrealistic piece of work.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks dress the words up as the title of Coward's ghost play; read separately they are two synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: Something whimsical and fanciful, lacking grounding in reality, gets this dismissive label meaning vague and unworkable.

clue.text: New bunch of keys outside for protection

indicators.note: outside says one group of letters wraps around the other

blocks.note: musical keys are named by letters, and these six are all valid key names
N is the standard abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Someone gets a fresh set of keys cut as a security measure.
explanation.walkthrough: Keys here are musical: D, E, F, C and E are each a key, so a bunch of them is a string of those letters around N.
explanation.definitionFit: Defence is shielding against attack or harm, the same as protection from danger.

clue.text: Members of church assist in finding girl's body

indicators.note: members are parts of a whole, so the letters are taken as part of the words that follow

blocks.note: runs across the end of the first word and most of the second

explanation.surface: Parishioners help to recover a missing girl's body.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads grimly like a murder search; the clue is lighter, using the slang sense of a woman's figure.
explanation.definitionFit: In old-fashioned slang the frame of a car became a jokey word for a woman's figure or physique.

clue.text: One for each child

blocks.note: per is Latin for for each, as in per head
a son is a child

explanation.surface: One portion is allotted for every child.
explanation.definitionFit: One as a pronoun stands for an individual human being, as in one never knows.

clue.text: I chop it, as ordered, for the ice-cream flavouring

indicators.note: as ordered says the letters are put into a new sequence as required

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written; it doubles as part of the indicator phrase

explanation.surface: A cook chops a nut as instructed to flavour ice cream.
explanation.definitionFit: The green nut is a classic gelato and ice-cream taste, popular across Italy and beyond.

clue.text: Tough Rugby enthusiast upset if embraced

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, so the letters run the other way
something embraced is held inside the arms of another word

blocks.note: RU is short for Rugby Union
a fan is an enthusiast
taken as written

explanation.surface: A hard-bitten rugby supporter gets upset if he is hugged.
explanation.walkthrough: Tough is a noun here, a hooligan, not the adjective the rugby surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough in this sense is a violent thug, and a ruffian is a brutal lawless person.

clue.text: Will a neat hedge do for this?

definitions.text: Will a neat hedge do for this?

blocks.note: surface reading: a gardener asks whether a trim hedge would serve as a boundary
setter's reading: split the answer as of plus a boundary word, so a hedge does in place of a fence; the printed count shows that split

explanation.surface: A gardener wonders whether a tidy hedge would be good enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The printed count (2-5) splits the answer as OF FENCE: a hedge does instead of a fence. The joined word, a cause of resentment, is what neighbours take over boundaries.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedge may stand in for a boundary wall, yet the whole word means an insult or cause of resentment.

clue.text: Chestnuts (chips off) for breakfast?

blocks.note: chestnuts are stale old jokes, and corn is trite, hackneyed material
a surface that flakes sheds small chips

explanation.surface: Roasted chestnuts with their shells chipped off are served at breakfast.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis looks like an aside about peeling nuts, but it supplies the second half of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The cereal is a typical breakfast dish, so the definition by example ends with a question mark.

clue.text: Flute of use to the military, if kept in iron case

definitions.text: Flute of use to the military

indicators.note: kept in says one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron, and case says it forms the outside
taken as written

explanation.surface: A military flute is stored in a metal case.
explanation.definitionFit: The small high-pitched transverse flute is played in military bands alongside drums, the classic marching instrument.

clue.text: Causing a body to pass through light?

definitions.text: Causing a body to pass through light?

blocks.clueFragment: Causing a body to pass through light
blocks.note: surface reading: a physics question about bodies travelling through light rays
setter's reading: a light is a window pane, so a person is thrown out through a window

explanation.surface: A physics puzzle about making an object travel through a beam of light.
explanation.walkthrough: Light is a window, as in a leaded light; the event famously occurred in Prague in 1618.
explanation.definitionFit: The term from Latin fenestra means throwing someone out of a window, a dramatic expulsion.

clue.text: Horsemen captured leader of Assyrian attackers

indicators.note: something captured is held within its captors
the leader of a word is its opening letter

blocks.note: riders are horsemen
the opening letter of the word Assyrian

explanation.surface: Mounted soldiers seize the commander of an invading Assyrian army.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiders make sudden hostile incursions, so they are attackers carrying out a raid.

clue.text: Hear score arranged for Nijinsky, for example

indicators.note: music that is arranged is reworked, so the letters are set out anew

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Listen to music orchestrated for the ballet dancer Nijinsky.
explanation.walkthrough: Nijinsky suggests the Russian dancer and ballet scores, but here he is the Triple Crown winner of 1970.
explanation.definitionFit: Nijinsky was a famous Irish-trained thoroughbred, winning the English Triple Crown in 1970.

clue.text: Gambler appearing in court endlessly

indicators.note: endlessly says the word loses its final letter

blocks.note: Chancery is a division of the English High Court

explanation.surface: A gambler keeps turning up in court without end.
explanation.walkthrough: Chancery is the Chancery Division of the High Court in England.
explanation.definitionFit: A chancer is an opportunist who takes risks hoping for a lucky break, much like a betting man.

clue.text: Resort is in place south of the Po

indicators.note: read as re-sort, it says the letters are sorted again into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A holiday resort sits in a spot below Italy's river Po.
explanation.walkthrough: Resort looks like a holiday town but is re-sort. The word describes Italy on the Roman side of the Alps, the Po valley region.
explanation.definitionFit: Cisalpine means on the Roman side of the Alps, the northern Italian lands around and below that river.

clue.text: Copper applied here to look after lowest parts of Hull, say?

definitions.text: Copper applied here to look after lowest parts of Hull, say?

blocks.clueFragment: Copper applied here to look after lowest parts of Hull
blocks.note: surface reading: a policeman posted to keep watch over the poorer districts of the city of Hull
setter's reading: copper sheathing is fixed to a ship's bottom at a place where vessels are kept out of the water

explanation.surface: A policeman is assigned to patrol the poorest neighbourhoods of Hull.
explanation.walkthrough: Hull is a port city in Yorkshire, but read as a ship's hull; copper plating protects the underside of wooden ships.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships are floated into an enclosed basin that is then pumped empty so the underwater body can be repaired.

clue.text: Playboy leaving with unearned profit

blocks.note: a rake is a dissolute pleasure-seeking man
someone who is leaving is off

explanation.surface: A playboy departs with ill-gotten gains.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut or commission taken, often dishonestly, from a deal is money gained without honest work.

clue.text: Day on river or trickling stream

blocks.note: D is the abbreviation for day
the Ribble is a river in Lancashire, north-west England

explanation.surface: A day spent by a river or a babbling brook.
explanation.walkthrough: River does not give R here but a named river; in a down clue 'on' places D above it.
explanation.definitionFit: A thin, unsteady flow of liquid is a trickle, the noun sense of this word.

clue.text: Directions for series of lectures

blocks.note: first meaning: routes or paths followed, as a ship sets several
second meaning: programmes of study, each a set of classes

explanation.surface: Instructions on how to find a lecture programme.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural noun means both the routes taken by ships and planned programmes of teaching sessions.

clue.text: Conservative drank up and applauded

blocks.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative
to lap is to drink with the tongue, as a cat does

explanation.surface: A Tory finished his drink and then cheered.
explanation.definitionFit: To clap is to strike the hands together in approval, the way an audience shows praise.

clue.text: Overthrow at Badminton, perhaps

blocks.note: surface reading: a shuttlecock hit too long in a game of badminton
setter's reading: the Badminton horse trials, where a rider may be thrown from the saddle

explanation.surface: A wild shot sails long in a badminton match.
explanation.walkthrough: Badminton Horse Trials are a famous eventing competition held in Gloucestershire, England, at Badminton House.
explanation.definitionFit: To throw a rider from the saddle, or figuratively to topple someone from power, is an overthrow.

clue.text: Tip of brass on silver made a successful conductor

indicators.note: a tip is an extreme end, here the final letter of the word

blocks.note: the final letter of the word brass
argent is silver, especially in heraldry

explanation.surface: A brass player's gratuity of silver coins made a conductor's career.
explanation.walkthrough: Tip suggests a gratuity and brass money, but it is the end letter of a word; in a down clue 'on' places it above.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Malcolm Sargent was a celebrated British conductor, long in charge of the Proms.

clue.text: Singles champion out of order?

blocks.note: surface reading: a tennis player who wins the singles title
setter's reading: an unmarried man of chivalry who belongs to no order of knighthood

explanation.surface: A tennis singles winner is disqualified for misconduct.
explanation.walkthrough: A champion is a knight, singles are unmarried men, and this grade of knighthood is the one not in any order such as the Garter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the most basic rank of British knighthood, conferred without membership of a chivalric order.

clue.text: Reversible slip

indicators.note: reversible says the word reads the same either way round

blocks.note: a blunder or mistake, spelt identically forwards and backwards

explanation.surface: A petticoat that can be worn inside out.
explanation.walkthrough: A slip is also an undergarment, which a reversible one would be; here it means an error.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a silly mistake or blunder, the same as a slip-up.

clue.text: Give thanks after harvest — size up again!

blocks.note: to reap is to harvest a crop
to praise God is to give thanks

explanation.surface: Farmers give thanks once the harvest is in, then take stock once more.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the thanks-giving word second, behind the harvest word.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise is to assess or evaluate, so doing it a second time means a fresh evaluation.

clue.text: Muscial interval before carnival is exhausted of vitality

blocks.note: E to F is a semitone, the smallest interval on a keyboard
a fete is a festive public celebration

explanation.surface: A musical interlude comes before the carnival is worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: Muscial is a typo for musical in the source. The interval is named by its two notes, E and F.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete describes something worn out and feeble, having lost its former vigour or strength.

clue.text: This fan is sticking fast

blocks.note: first meaning: a follower or supporter of a cause
second meaning: as an adjective, clinging or attached firmly

explanation.surface: A loyal supporter refuses to budge.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a devoted follower, and the adjective describes something glued firmly in place.
